---
title: Password protection
---

Static hosting does not normally have a login system. A limited password gate
can nevertheless be added to selected Quarto output by encrypting its rendered
HTML with [StatiCrypt](https://github.com/robinmoisson/staticrypt) before the
site is deployed.

The `structure_biology` project uses this pattern for its complete instructor
site. Student material remains at the site root, scheduled solutions are
published below `/solution/`, and the password-gated instructor version is
published below `/instructor/`.

For the surrounding setup, see [Quarto profiles](profiles.qmd),
[Release scheduling](scheduling.qmd), and
[GitHub Pages & Actions](github-pages.qmd).

::: {.callout-warning title="A convenience gate, not access control"}
StatiCrypt is useful for discouraging casual browsing, but it does not add
users, permissions, revocation, or server-side authorization to GitHub Pages.
Do not use this pattern for confidential, personal, regulated, or
assessment-sensitive material that requires real access control.
:::

## How the publication flow works

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    A["Render all Quarto profiles"] --> B["Set up Node.js"]
    B --> C["Encrypt instructor HTML with StatiCrypt"]
    C --> D["Verify protected and public outputs"]
    D --> E["Upload the combined Pages artifact"]
    E --> F["Deploy to GitHub Pages"]
```

StatiCrypt replaces each selected HTML file with a page containing an
encrypted copy of the original document, a password form, and browser-side
decryption code. The visitor enters the shared password and the browser
decrypts the page. No application server is involved.

Encryption belongs after the final Quarto render and before the Pages artifact
is uploaded. If Quarto runs afterward, it overwrites the encrypted files with
ordinary HTML.

## Create a separate instructor profile

Give the protected profile its own output directory. Restricting it to HTML
also avoids presenting PDF or Word downloads that StatiCrypt will not encrypt:

```yaml
# course_notes/_quarto-instructor.yml
project:
  output-dir: _site/instructor

website:
  navbar:
    right:
      - href: ../index.html
        text: Go to student version
      - href: ../solution/index.html
        text: Go to solution version

format-links: false

teaching:
  show-solutions: true
  default-solution-title: "Solution"
```

The base Quarto configuration should select HTML as its default format. The
instructor profile must not add unencrypted output formats. Render all profiles
into a combined tree before encryption:

```toml
# pixi.toml
[tasks.render-all]
cmd = "quarto render course_notes --profile student,publish && quarto render course_notes --profile solution,publish && quarto render course_notes --profile instructor,publish"
depends-on = ["clean"]

[tasks.clean]
cmd = "rm -rf course_notes/_site"
```

The order matters because the student render creates `_site`, while the later
renders add `/solution/` and `/instructor/` beneath it.

## Keep a stable StatiCrypt salt

Generate the StatiCrypt configuration once from the repository root:

```bash
npx --yes staticrypt@3.5.4 --salt
```

This creates `.staticrypt.json` with a random salt:

```json
{
  "salt": "replace-with-the-generated-32-character-hex-value"
}
```

Commit this file. The salt is not a password and does not need to be secret;
it is also embedded in the encrypted output. Keeping it stable allows
StatiCrypt's **Remember me** option to recognize the same password across
different instructor pages and later deployments. Changing or deleting the
salt signs remembered users out.

By default, visitors can select **Remember me**, which stores a salted and
hashed password value in browser local storage. Use `--remember false` in the
encryption command if this option should not be offered on shared computers.

## Choose where the password is stored

There are two reasonable patterns, depending on what the gate is meant to do.

### Repository-visible shared password

For a public teaching repository, the Quarto source is already readable by
anyone who finds the repository. A visible password can therefore be an
intentional, low-complexity way to discourage learners from casually entering
an instructor URL:

```yaml
env:
  STATICRYPT_PASSWORD: "replace-with-a-long-shared-course-password"
```

This is the pattern used by `structure_biology`. Do not reuse an institutional,
personal, or otherwise sensitive password. Anyone who can read the workflow
can read this value.

### GitHub Actions repository secret

Use a repository secret when the source is private, or when the password
should not be immediately visible in the workflow:

```yaml
env:
  STATICRYPT_PASSWORD: ${{ secrets.STATICRYPT_PASSWORD }}
```

In the repository on GitHub, open **Settings → Secrets and variables →
Actions**, select **New repository secret**, and create
`STATICRYPT_PASSWORD`. GitHub documents this process in
[Using secrets in GitHub Actions](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/how-tos/write-workflows/choose-what-workflows-do/use-secrets).

An unavailable secret expands to an empty value, so the workflow should fail
before encryption rather than wait for an interactive password prompt. A
secret hides the value from the workflow and masks it in ordinary logs, but it
does not provide per-user access or prevent recipients from sharing it.

## Encrypt during the Pages workflow

Add the following steps to the existing build job after Quarto renders the
site and before the Pages artifact is uploaded. The example uses a repository
secret; substitute the visible `env` value above for an intentionally public
convenience password.

```yaml
- name: Set up Node for StatiCrypt
  uses: actions/setup-node@v5
  with:
    node-version: 24

- name: Encrypt instructor site
  env:
    STATICRYPT_PASSWORD: ${{ secrets.STATICRYPT_PASSWORD }}
  run: |
    test -n "$STATICRYPT_PASSWORD"
    test -f course_notes/_site/instructor/index.html
    npx --yes staticrypt@3.5.4 course_notes/_site/instructor/* \
      --recursive \
      --directory course_notes/_site/instructor \
      --config .staticrypt.json \
      --short \
      --template-title "Course name — instructor"

- name: Verify encrypted output
  run: |
    grep -q 'staticrypt' course_notes/_site/instructor/index.html
    ! grep -q 'complete instructor version' \
      course_notes/_site/instructor/index.html
    ! grep -q 'staticrypt' course_notes/_site/index.html
```

Pinning the Node and StatiCrypt versions makes publication reproducible. The
input glob selects the contents of the instructor directory, `--recursive`
processes nested pages, and `--directory` writes the transformed tree back to
the same location. The configuration path points StatiCrypt to the committed
salt. `--short` only suppresses StatiCrypt's short-password warning; it does
not shorten or otherwise alter the password.

The compact verification step confirms that the instructor landing page was
transformed, recognizable instructor plaintext is absent, and the public
landing page was not encrypted. Replace the example plaintext with a stable
phrase that is genuinely present in the project's instructor page. For a
stricter workflow, apply the same checks to a known nested instructor page.

## Test the protected output locally

Ordinary Quarto previews should remain unencrypted so maintainers can edit and
debug the instructor version quickly. Test the production behavior separately:

```bash
pixi run render-all
export STATICRYPT_PASSWORD="temporary-local-test-password"
npx --yes staticrypt@3.5.4 course_notes/_site/instructor/* \
  --recursive \
  --directory course_notes/_site/instructor \
  --config .staticrypt.json \
  --short \
  --template-title "Course name — instructor"
python -m http.server --directory course_notes/_site
```

Open `http://localhost:8000/instructor/` and test both an incorrect and the
correct password. StatiCrypt 3 uses browser WebCrypto and therefore needs an
HTTPS or localhost context; opening the generated HTML directly as a local
file is not a representative test. Run the project's clean task afterward to
remove the locally encrypted output before the next render.

Also inspect at least one nested instructor page, the unprotected student and
solution sites, and any instructor downloads. Non-HTML files are copied rather
than encrypted and can be requested directly if their URLs are known.

## Rotate and share the password

To rotate a repository-visible password, edit the workflow. To rotate a
secret, update `STATICRYPT_PASSWORD` in the repository's Actions secrets. In
both cases, trigger a complete publication workflow: existing pages remain
decryptable with the old password until the new encrypted artifact is
successfully deployed.

Share the password through an appropriate course communication channel, not in
the public website. Rotation changes one shared credential for everyone; it
cannot revoke one person's access. A recipient can also redistribute the
password or retain material after decrypting it.

## Understand the security boundary

StatiCrypt encrypts the selected rendered HTML, but it does not hide:

- Quarto source and repository history in a public repository.
- Images, datasets, PDFs, notebooks, and other non-HTML assets.
- The existence and path of `/instructor/`, filenames, or link targets.
- Content copied, downloaded, or screenshotted after decryption.
- A password that is committed directly to the workflow.

GitHub Pages is available from private repositories on eligible paid plans,
but GitHub states that the published Pages site is still publicly available.
See [Creating a GitHub Pages site](https://docs.github.com/en/pages/getting-started-with-github-pages/creating-a-github-pages-site)
and [Securing a Pages site with HTTPS](https://docs.github.com/en/pages/getting-started-with-github-pages/securing-your-github-pages-site-with-https).
A private repository plus a secret prevents casual access to the source and
password, but visitors still receive the encrypted page from a public URL.

Use an authenticated hosting service with server-side authorization when
access must be assigned to named users, audited, or revoked individually.
